content: Environmental microbiology is the scientific study of the composition and physiological characteristics of microbial communities in various environments. These environments include soil, water, air, and sediments that cover the Earth, as well as the plants and animals that inhabit these areas. Additionally, environmental microbiology encompasses the study of microorganisms that exist in artificial environments, such as bioreactors. Microbial life is extraordinarily diverse, with microorganisms found in virtually every corner of the planet. It is estimated that less than 1% of microbial species on Earth have been identified. Microorganisms are capable of surviving in some of the most extreme environments, such as high-temperature habitats exceeding 100°C, including geysers, hydrothermal vents (black smokers), and oil wells. Other microbes thrive in extremely cold habitats, highly saline environments, or acidic and alkaline waters. For example, the Archaea are a group of microorganisms known for their ability to survive in such extreme conditions. A single gram of soil contains approximately one billion microorganisms, representing potentially thousands of species. Microorganisms play a critical role in the biosphere, serving as the foundation of ecosystems in areas where sunlight cannot penetrate. In these zones, chemosynthetic bacteria provide energy and carbon to other organisms by utilizing chemical compounds. Some microbes act as decomposers, recycling nutrients, while others play essential roles in biogeochemical cycles. Bacteria, in particular, are vital due to their symbiotic relationships with other organisms, which can have both positive and negative effects on ecosystems. Microorganisms are also employed in in-situ microbial biodegradation or bioremediation processes to treat domestic, agricultural, and industrial wastes, as well as subsurface pollution in soils, sediments, and marine environments. The ability of a microorganism to degrade toxic waste depends on the specific nature of the contaminant. Since most polluted sites contain multiple types of pollutants, the most effective approach to microbial biodegradation involves using a mixture of bacterial species and strains, each specialized in degrading one or more types of contaminants. Monitoring the composition of both indigenous and introduced bacteria is crucial to evaluate their activity levels and to adjust nutrient and environmental conditions to optimize the bioremediation process. Petroleum oil is highly toxic, and oil pollution in the environment, such as oil spills in coastal regions and open seas, poses significant ecological challenges. While oil spills are difficult to contain and mitigate, much of the oil can be degraded by the hydrocarbon-degrading activities of microbial communities, particularly hydrocarbonoclastic bacteria (HCB). These bacteria play a key role in remediating the ecological damage caused by oil pollution in marine habitats. Additionally, HCB have potential biotechnological applications, such as in the production of bioplastics and biocatalysis. Certain strains of the bacterium Acinetobacter, isolated from the environment, are capable of biodegrading a wide range of aromatic compounds. The predominant pathway for the final stages of assimilation into central metabolites involves catechol or protocatechuate (3,4-dihydroxybenzoate) and the beta-ketoadipate pathway. The diversity within the Acinetobacter genus lies in its ability to channel growth substrates, many of which are natural products of plant origin, into this metabolic pathway. Biotreatment, the processing of waste materials using living organisms, is an environmentally friendly alternative to conventional waste treatment methods. Bioreactors have been developed to address the limitations of biotreatment processes by providing highly controlled systems. The versatility of bioreactor design allows for the treatment of a wide range of waste materials under optimized conditions. It is essential to consider the diversity of microorganisms involved, and extensive analyses are often required to ensure effective waste treatment. The application of molecular biology and genomics to environmental microbiology has revealed a remarkable complexity in natural microbial communities. Techniques such as diversity surveys, community fingerprinting, and functional interrogation of natural populations have become common, facilitated by advancements in molecular and bioinformatics tools. Recent studies on the ecology of cyanobacteria have explored various habitats, demonstrating that cyanobacterial communities are often habitat-specific and that significant genetic diversity exists among morphologically simple types. The integration of molecular, bioinformatics, physiological, and geochemical techniques has advanced the study of natural cyanobacterial communities.
